newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo shares drop after Dow, dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo shares drop after Dow, dollar falls.

text.p: Tokyo shares dropped sharply on Monday, spooked by Friday's sell-off on Wall Street and a weaker dollar against the yen.
In late afternoon trade, the benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares was down more than 700 points, or more than 3.5 percent, to below 19,000 points, its lowest level since April 30.
The dollar was trading at around 115 yen after its nosedive on Friday in overseas markets, despite having firmed in Tokyo morning trade against the yen and other major currencies.

"Investors were losing faith in the (Japanese) economy following economic data that showed the recovery was not coming along as expected," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities. "Then the Dow and the dollar fell, giving more participants cold feet and inviting more selling."
On Friday in New York, the Dow industrials slid 156.78 points to end at 8,031.22, the ninth-largest point decline on record.
"A depressed mood spread in the market, especially in blue chips, due to the sharp fall in New York and the yen's advance," said a broker at a "Big Four" securities house.
Export-oriented issues were especially hard-hit, since a lower dollar against the Japanese yen reduces the value of profits earned by Japanese companies abroad.
Renewed problems in Japan's securities industry over payoffs to corporate racketeers did not appear to be a factor in the market's slide.

Shares in Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, the third major Japanese financial firm to push out senior management over the scandal, were up 35 yen at 264 yen in mid-afternoon trade, a gain of more than 15 percent.

Yamaichi said on Monday that its chairman, president and nine other top executives were resigning to take responsibility for the scandal, which has also ensnared Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.
Industry analysts said the shares were buoyed by investor relief over the reshuffle.
In afternoon Tokyo the dollar was trading at slightly above 115 yen, higher than its close of 114.80 yen in New York on Friday but well below a level of around 118 seen in Asia last week.
"Japanese importers, such as oil companies, apparently came to their offices earlier than usual and bought dollars for yen," said a Japanese trust bank trader.

Some traders said the reversal for the dollar was merely a correction from its recent run-up to 119 yen. But dealers said there is also some concern about the high-flying U.S. stock market, which is in turn putting pressure on the dollar.
Japanese government bonds were little changed in choppy trading after rising earlier in the day on the back of falling share prices.
